input: Brainstorm a name for my new bakery

candidate.taskDescription: Generate a unique and appealing name for your new bakery.

questions.title: What type of bakery do you envision (e.g., traditional, modern, artisanal, vegan)?
questions.description: Consider the vibe you want to create.

questions.title: Who is your target customer base (e.g., young professionals, families, health-conscious individuals)?
questions.description: Understand their preferences and needs.

questions.title: What unique selling proposition (USP) do you want your bakery to highlight (e.g., organic ingredients, gluten-free options, artisanal pastries)?
questions.description: Identify what makes your bakery stand out.

questions.title: Do you have any specific themes or inspirations for the bakery's name (e.g., nature, culture, personal interests)?
questions.description: Think about any motifs or inspirations that resonate with you.

questions.title: What word or phrase do you feel best represents the essence of your bakery (e.g., 'Sweet Haven', 'Artisan Delight', 'Wholesome Bites')?
questions.description: Choose a word that captures the spirit you want to convey.

questions.title: How long do you want the bakery name to be (e.g., 1-3 words, 4-6 words)?
questions.description: Consider the readability and memorability of the name.

questions.title: Are there any names or words that you absolutely cannot use (e.g., family names, trademarked terms)?
questions.description: Be mindful of any restrictions or preferences.

verdict.notes: SET B's phrasing is robotic and over-engineered — parenthetical examples in every question make it feel like a survey form rather than a human coach. Questions 3 and 5 substantially overlap (both fish for name concepts/words), and Q1 and Q2 partially duplicate A's cleaner versions without adding meaningful depth; notably, B never asks about personal story/owner connection, location, or desired tone/vibe as a standalone question, which are key creative inputs A covers more naturally.

questions.description: Air conditioning, navigation, sunroof, etc.

questions.title: Have you driven any cars recently?
questions.description: This will help you assess your current driving skills.

questions.title: What is your timeline for purchasing the car?
questions.description: How soon do you need the car?

verdict.notes: Set B has vague, generic questions ("driving preference," "Have you driven any cars recently?") that don't meaningfully inform used-car planning, and misses critical unknowns like acceptable mileage, vehicle age/year range, and geographic search area. Set A is more concrete and action-oriented for this specific task.

questions.description: e.g., nearby, weekday/weekend

questions.title: Do you have any specific concerns or issues you want to address?
questions.description: e.g., anxiety, depression, relationship problems

questions.title: What is your budget for therapy sessions?
questions.description: e.g., per session, monthly fee

questions.title: Do you prefer online therapy or in-person sessions?
questions.description: e.g., both, only in-person

verdict.notes: Set B combines two asks in Q3 ("location and availability"), wastes a slot on prior therapy history (not directly actionable for planning), and misses key practical unknowns like who the therapy is for and urgency of the first appointment. Questions 1 and 4 also overlap significantly — type of therapy and specific concerns are closely related, reducing non-redundancy.

verdict.notes: Set B wastes a question asking about rescheduling/cancelling (irrelevant to booking a new appointment) and misses key unknowns like urgency and who the appointment is for. Q1 ("what type of doctor appointment") is oddly generic given the user already said "GP," and Q3 ("are you able to travel") is an awkward proxy for the in-person vs. remote question that Set A handles more naturally.

Do you have a preferred learning method (e.g., online lessons, guitar tutor, self-study)?
How many hours per week are you able to dedicate to practice?

verdict.notes: Set B wastes a question asking about joining a guitar community (a suggestion, not a clarifying question) and conflates skill level with prior musical experience across two overlapping questions (Q1 and Q5). input: Update my resume for a product manager role

candidate.taskDescription: I need to modify my resume to better reflect my qualifications and experiences for a product manager position.

questions.title: Which specific product management roles or industries are you targeting?
questions.description: To tailor my resume effectively.

questions.title: What skills and experiences do you want to highlight most prominently on my resume?
questions.description: To ensure my resume aligns with the job description.

questions.description: To include relevant examples.

questions.description: To adjust my resume accordingly.

questions.title: Which industries or companies are you applying to for this role?
questions.description: To customize my resume for each application.

questions.title: Do you have any specific keywords or phrases you would like me to include in my resume?
questions.description: To optimize for Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) and job postings.

questions.title: What is your preferred format for the resume (e.g., chronological, functional, hybrid)?
questions.description: To ensure the resume is easy to read and highlight my strengths.

candidate.taskTitle: Update my resume for a product manager role

verdict.notes: Set B has a glaring redundancy issue — questions 1 and 5 both ask about target industries/companies, wasting a slot. It also omits two critical unknowns that Set A covers well: whether the user has an existing resume to work from, and their timeline. The phrasing in Q2 also incorrectly uses "my resume" (first-person slip), and the keyword/format questions feel generic rather than task-critical.

verdict.notes: Set B is largely generic and could apply to almost any administrative task — it never asks about German-specific details (Finanzamt, residency status, employment type, Steuer-ID), which are essential for planning German tax filing. Questions 5 and 7 are especially vague filler, and Q2 and Q3 partially overlap with each other (professional help vs. goal). Set A is far more concrete and actionable for this specific task.
